method: Re-ran the brief's walk() verbatim at step 0.25 m on all four published segment lists; independently recomputed closure, final heading, plan length, bounding box, merged straight runs, merged full-throttle runs (straights joined across any corner of centreline radius >= 80 m, which the brief's own vocabulary calls 'a direction change not a corner'), cyclic minimum separation over pairs more than 40 m apart along the lap, edge-to-edge clear ground using each segment's own width_m, elevation closure and range, and the elevation difference at each layout's closest pair. Re-derived the pit-lane racing-line arguments from corner sense in both directions. Every number below is from my own run unless it is attributed to a layout or to its verifier.
ranking_note: The top three are inside two points and every one of them earned 'major issues'. The ordering is by cost-to-legal, not by polish: rhythm's defects are edits to fields (raise two vertical radii, relabel one cliff claim, delete one invented distance, fix one sum) and move no control point. Racecraft's require re-solving the free straight lengths against the vertical-curve schedule, which moves plan geometry, plus tightening T6 and T7, which rewrites the overtaking case. Terrain's require adding plan length in two places, one of which pushes Il Salto past the 200 m cap and therefore forces a new corner into the layout. Instrument's require opening its closest pair from 20.56 m to roughly 32 m, which is a re-solve of the entire loop, plus relocating both pit junctions.

scores.strongest: The only layout that reads 'the value of R must be adequately increased along approach, release, braking and curved sections' as a number rather than a sentence. Every vertical curve is sized at 1.3x to 2.5x its regulation minimum by stated policy - VC1 1,600 m against 1,130 (1.42x), VC2 900 against 471 (1.91x), VC3 1,300 against 971 (1.34x) - and the author states what it cost: roughly 3 m of available elevation range, which is why the range is 7.393 m and not 10-11 m. It is also the only start line in the set with no vertical curve within 150 m in either direction, on purpose, so eight karts do a standing start on one plane. Nobody else paid for the article; rhythm paid and published the invoice.
scores.weakest: The reverse-layout vertical claim is geometrically false and it is load-bearing. 'Every one of the six vertical curves swaps profile when the direction reverses - a crest becomes a valley' is wrong: d2z/ds2 is invariant under s -> L-s, so a crest is a crest driven either way and K does not change. The reverse minima it publishes (847.4 / 627.8 / 728.5 / 767.7 / 317.6 / 627.5 m) are computed by swapping K=15 and K=20 and are not the requirement. Under the correct test VC2 (concave, R=900 m) sits inside the author's own 41.5 m reverse uphill braking zone at their own stated ~138 km/h, needing 138^2/20 = 952.2 m. 900 < 952. 'Checked, all six pass' is not true, and what actually saves four of the other five is the margin policy, not the check.
scores.reasoning:
Hard compliance 13/20: length 1367.2 in band; start straight 164.65 m at +0.60% (cap 2%); 87.5 m to the first corner and 77.15 m from the last, so both directions clear the 50 m and 70 m minima on the same physical line; first corner 100 deg at 12.0 m; min width 9 m; banking peaks at 9% against a 10% cap, the closest of the four but legal. Against it: the longest geometric straight is 186.68 m and legal, but T2 is R=90 m through 45 deg with a 186 m line radius and 0.78 g - by the brief's own vocabulary not a corner - so the actual continuous full-throttle run is 354.5 m, 77% over the cap and the worst defeat of that rule in the set. The author names it ('a legal necessity dressed as a corner... a reviewer is entitled to call it filler'), which is honesty, not compliance. Pit-lane forward geometry survives my own frame check: T8b is -85 deg and T1 is -100 deg, both lefts, both exits track the kart to the right edge, and both junctions are on the left. The reverse pit lane is never analysed - the 22 deg deceleration branch becomes a 158 deg merge driven the other way, over the 30 deg cap, exactly as racecraft states for its own lane.

Geometry 8/15: closure 0.000478 m by the brief's walk - but rhythm.json reports 0.000208 m while rhythm.md's own receipt reports 0.000478, so the JSON publishes a number that is not the measurement. Half a millimetre is immaterial; publishing an unreproducible measurement in an ADR-0046 source file is not. Min separation 30.924 m, at T3's own turn-in and exit tangents, 40.07 m apart along the lap - i.e. 0.07 m outside the brief's own exemption window. Five corners exceed the 1.86 g ceiling on the centreline at their claimed apex (T1 1.988, T4 2.623, T5 2.223, T7 2.030, T8a 1.965); T4's 2.62 g is the worst centreline demand anywhere in the four proposals, and a probe that follows the spline reads it as impossible. T4's headline claim is also wrong in the direction that matters: 100.0 km/h is the GRIP ceiling at a 42.5 m line radius, the LOCK ceiling is 94.88 km/h, so T4 sits 5.1 km/h PAST #137's boundary rather than on it - and 12 of the document's other 13 lock ceilings reproduce to 0.1 km/h, so this is the single exception and it is the one carrying a conclusion. Reversed T8's 132 km/h turn-in, the number the whole reverse layout rests on, gets no radius arithmetic at all.

Elevation 13/20: closes to -1e-05 m against a 0.05 m gate; range 7.393 m, the smallest of the four and derived rather than chosen; six gradient changes, all with a stated chosen radius above the minimum and a stated clearance to the nearest corner and braking zone. Docked 7 for the K-swap error above, which makes the reverse compliance claim untrue.

Run-off 12/15: the >80 deg rule is honoured on all six qualifying changes (T1 100, T3 140, T4 90, T5 85, T6 via its 85 deg apex arc, T7 90, T8 via its 85 deg exit arc) with compound totals used correctly. It is the only layout that states the scaling law it used - T7 is sized by v^2 against T1's 138 km/h, 'a factor of 2.35, not the 1.53 a linear rule would give' - and the only one that sizes a corner twice, once per layout: T8 gets 8 m asphalt + 14 m grass against 106 km/h forward and 12 m + 26 m against 132 km/h reversed, on the same axis. T3 says plainly that the stated width is not the output of the art 7.5 simulation. Against it: T5's run-off restriction is invented. The claimed 18.4 m to Link T7-T8 is 152.645 m measured; the closest thing to the T4-T5 esse is 71.53 m. The barrier-instead-of-depth decision it justifies has no basis, and T5's inside has 150 m of clear land.

Footprint 6/10: 418.5 x 344.3 m = 14.41 ha of bounding box for 1,367 m of track, 94.9 m of lap per hectare - the largest box for the least relief in the set. With a 36 m run-off and verge belt the land requirement is about 490 x 416 m = 20.4 ha, paddock inside the loop. That is a large property for a kart circuit; a 1,200-1,300 m European Grade 1 track typically sits on 10-15 ha. The author says it himself: 'a low track density - a lot of empty ground to dress'.

Buildability 7/10: 25 segments, 14,547 m2 of ribbon (the largest), 11 width changes across 9-12 m, but 7.393 m of relief (the smallest) and no bespoke structure anywhere - no retaining wall, no highwall, no made ground. Middle cost overall. The specific pipeline enemy here is the 354.5 m of near-zero-curvature road: a long low-curvature ribbon plus a lightmap bake is where grazing-angle seams and wasted lumels come from, and it is 26% of the lap.

Validatability 6/10: the forward geometry is the easiest of the four to check - closure 0.5 mm, min separation 30.9 m, no 3D separation problem, one elevation profile. But the document hands a validator a rule that is wrong. A check written from rhythm's own reverse section would swap K, bless VC2 and VC5, and pass a reverse layout that is not legal. That is ADR-0046's failure mode exactly: the file loads, the gate goes green, and the reverse layout cannot be raced to the regulation.

scores.strongest: Two things, and both are regulation work nobody else did. First, the pit lane: it is the only one of four whose forward junction geometry survives my own independent frame check without argument - T7 is a right-hander so the approach line runs down the left edge and the deceleration lane peels right at s=1100; T1 is a right-hander so the entry line is on the left and the exit lane rejoins the right edge at s=40. And it is the only document that works out that a pit lane does not reverse: 'the deceleration lane leaves at 25 deg to the direction of travel; driven the other way that same asphalt is a 155 deg merge, and Part 1 section 7.2 caps the angle at 30 deg. The reverse layout needs its OWN entry and exit stubs - that is geometry, not furniture.' All four layouts have that defect. One of them found it. Second, the general result: a_vert at the legal minimum vertical radius is K/12.96 m/s2 REGARDLESS of speed, because a_vert = v^2/R and R_min = V^2/K. So the maximum load swing a legal Grade 1 kart circuit can ever produce is -11.8% over any crest and +15.7% in any compression, at any speed, before the article's 'increase R near braking and curves' takes it down further. That belongs in ARCHITECTURE section 11.
scores.weakest: The document publishes two elevation profiles and they are different roads. The per-segment grade list closes to -5.116e-05 m with a 14.5872 m range - correct, and the number reported in `measured`. Integrating the eight published vertical curves at their published stations and transition lengths does NOT close: +0.601189 m of error against a 0.05 m gate, with a 12.624 m range, and the two disagree by up to 2.0947 m. The author reported the one that passes. For this pipeline that is not a bookkeeping nit: gentrack.py sweeps a ribbon along a spline and needs one z(s). This file cannot supply one, and ADR-0046 says track.json owns the whole track. Compounding it, the crest at s=475.7 is chosen at 950 m against a stated 908 m minimum - 4.6% of margin, the tightest vertical curve in all four proposals - and that 908 m is worked from a T2 apex speed the verifier shows is understated. At the corrected station speed of 132.0 km/h the requirement is 1,161 m and the chosen 950 m is 18% under the legal minimum, in a release section 30 m past a corner exit, which is precisely where art 7.2 says increase R.
scores.reasoning:
Hard compliance 14/20: length 1302.56; start/finish straight 198.0 m, inside both the 120-200 m starting-straight band and the 200 m longest-straight cap with 2.0 m to spare, and the line placed so that BOTH directions clear 50 m to the first corner and 70 m from the last on the same asphalt (110 m and 88 m) - the cleanest bidirectional start-line solve of the four. First corner 98 deg at 12.0 m. Min width 9 m, camber 2.0%, banking 3-6%, no adverse camber. Pit forward correct as above; reverse pit disclosed as broken rather than claimed working. Docked for the 200 m cap being met in the letter and defeated in effect: T5 is R=90 m through 30 deg with a 349.63 m line radius, which is not a corner at all, so segments 10+11+12 form a 237.79 m continuously flat run, and the verifier's independent profile finds a 380 m run with no braking event because T6 is also flat. Verge width, edge-line width and run-off cross-slope appear nowhere as fields.

Geometry 7/15: closure 0.001026 m reproduced exactly, heading +360.000, no self-intersection, min separation 30.398 m (the author reports 30.476 - optimistic by 0.08 m) with 20.4 m of clear ground. But two of the nine 'corners' do not corner. T5's geometric maximum line radius is 349.63 m and T6's is 121.56 m, which at 1.86 g is 169.5 km/h - above the kart's top speed, so T6 is flat out, and the document's claim that it is 'the fastest corner on the circuit without run-off' at 119.1 km/h with an 8.4 m braking zone does not exist on the published geometry. T7's claimed 94.2 km/h, the premise of the whole concertina-onto-the-start-straight argument, is 107-109 km/h on its own 49.98 m line. And T5's apex is published at 143.9 km/h - the kart's measured FLAT-GROUND top speed - at the apex of a corner on a +4.38% climb, contradicted by the same document's own 137.8 km/h forward top speed and its own prose ('taken flat at 116-126 km/h'). Every defensive-penalty number in the proposal uses the inside-EDGE radius where a pinned defender actually drives the largest arc fitting the inner half: 51.50 m not 27 m at T1, 73.53 m not 26.5 m at T6. The claimed penalties are 2x to 30x overstated, and at T1 the author's own free-line radius (48.85 m) is SMALLER than the correct pinned line (51.50 m), so in the author's own frame the defender is faster than the attacker. The racing character is unsupported by the geometry that was published.

Elevation 9/20: the dual-profile failure above is worth most of the deduction; the 950 m crest is the rest. Credit retained for the K/12.96 derivation, for placing all eight vertical curves inside straights and none inside a corner - the only layout in the set that manages that - and for raising the s=195 curve 57% over its minimum because it sits in a release section, which is the article read correctly at one of eight places.

Run-off 13/15, the best in the set: it is the only layout that publishes a stopping calculation per corner rather than a width. Gravel at an assumed 0.80 g, departure angle 12-15 deg on fast corners and 90 deg on the hairpin, required width against built width: T1 14.1 m required / 15 m built, T2 13.9 / 15, T3 17.3 / 20, T4 11.1 / 14, T7 11.3 / 12. The >80 deg rule is applied to the COMPOUND direction change, which is the correct reading and which two other layouts get right only by accident: T1 is 50+48 = 98 deg and T2 is 48+52 = 100 deg, both mandatory. T5 (30 deg) and T6 (50 deg) are correctly exempt, and T6 is given 10 m anyway because it is fast. And the honest limit at T4 is stated in full: a total brake failure arrives at 136.6 km/h forward and 143.7 km/h reversed, needing 91.7 m and 101.5 m of gravel, which is not buildable and is not built. Docked 2 because the two constants the whole calculation rests on - 0.80 g gravel and the departure angles - are engineering judgement rather than measurement, which the author says himself, and because the verge appears only inside corner prose.

Footprint 8/10: 377.5 x 331.7 m = 12.52 ha of box, 104 m of lap per hectare, about 428 x 382 m = 16.3 ha with a 25 m belt and the pit and paddock inside the T7 loop. That is a realistic property. The 14.587 m elevation range is the largest of the four and it is the only one with a named physical source - a worked-out sand quarry, plateau to floor - so the relief is not a taste call.

Buildability 7/10, and it is the cheapest of the four to build: 17 segments (8 straights, 9 corners - fewest of anything in the set), 12,244 m2 of ribbon (smallest), 9-12 m of width over 8 changes, run-off no wider than 20 m. Roughly 10-15% cheaper than instrument or terrain on ribbon and bake area and about 25% cheaper than terrain on dressed ground. Two things claw it back. Every taper in the design (9->12 into T1, 12->9->12 along the back straight, 9->10 into T4, 10->9 out of T7) exists only inside prose `note` strings while each segment carries one scalar width_m, so the ribbon gentrack.py would actually sweep is not the ribbon that was verified. And the sweeper cannot be handed a z(s) at all until somebody decides which of the two published profiles is the road.

Validatability 6/10: second hardest. A validator must first choose between two elevation profiles before it can check anything vertical - and ADR-0046 says the file owns the track, so the file being self-contradictory is a source-of-truth problem, not a rounding problem. The straight-length check passes at 198 m while the thing that rule exists to cap is a 380 m full-throttle run, so a geometric check is the wrong check. Credit for being the only file that enumerates what a reverse validator would have to catch about its own pit lane.

scores.strongest: It is the only layout whose longest straight is also its longest continuous full-throttle run - 196.92 m, both, because no corner on the circuit has a centreline radius above 65 m and therefore nothing on the lap is a straight pretending to be a corner. Instrument runs 219.9 m flat out, racecraft 237.8 m (380 m by its verifier's own profile), rhythm 354.5 m. Terrain alone lets the 200 m cap do the job it exists to do. Second: T7's run-off is the best single piece of site reasoning in all four documents. It is a mandatory axial run-off on a 90 deg direction change (45+45 compound, correctly totalled), the axis points straight up the hill into the quarry's old highwall, and the run-off is therefore free from the landform - 6 m of apron graded to the art 7.5 10% cap, 22 m of rising gravel, tire barrier against the rock. Third: the elevation range is derived, not chosen. 11.42 m is exactly what 146.3 m of return climb at 7.81% can pay for, and 146.3 m is what the 200 m straight cap allows, so the number falls out of two regulations meeting.
scores.weakest: The layout is sold on its elevation and the vertical work is the worst-executed of the four - three separate overlap failures, one of them an 18x overstatement, and a flat compliance claim that is false. Forward: La Conca is 41.98 m and the author's stated margin is +1.5 m for the compression's 36.7 m of vertical curve plus 3.8 m of braking for T3. The braking arithmetic is wrong by 2.3x - 138 -> 125 km/h at 1.53 g is 8.79 m, not 3.8 - so the true margin is -3.48 m and the vertical curve is inside T3's braking zone. Reverse: the two Il Salto curves OVERLAP by 13.21 m, and the claimed '31 m lead-in between them' is 1.729 m of actual constant-grade road, because the first curve eats 7.67 m of the 30.98 m band and the second eats the rest. Reverse T2's braking zone still overlaps a vertical curve by 8.92 m - the exact defect the author's what_breaks says was fixed; it went from 11.4 m to 8.9 m. And all six curves are at exactly R = V^2/K by explicit written policy ('Both compressions on this circuit are built at the minimum radius... There was no reason not to') while five of six sit in a section art 7.2 names by name. There is a reason: that article. 'All six vertical curves pass in reverse as well as forwards. Both directions now pass' is not true.
scores.reasoning:
Hard compliance 15/20, the best of the four on the hard gates: length 1340.97, closure 0.017 m (largest of the set but 60x inside the 1 m gate, and disclosed as 0.01 m rounding on a least-squares solve), heading +360.000, min separation 34.288 m with 24.3 m of clear ground - the widest margin anywhere in the set. Longest straight 196.92 m plan and 197.197 m measured the way art 11 measures official length, so 2.80 m of margin rather than the 3.08 the author quotes. Start straight 188.265 m at -0.70% - and the reason it is on the bench rather than the pan is that the bench is the only terrace long enough to hold a 120-200 m starting straight inside the 2% gradient cap, which is a regulation driving a plan decision rather than decorating one. 113.13 m to the first corner and 75.13 m from the last, so both directions clear. Min width 9 m, camber 2.0-2.5%, banking 4-7%. Deducted for taking three boundaries at exactly zero tolerance: T1 is exactly 45.0 deg (the floor of 'the first corner is by definition a direction change >= 45 deg') and exactly 12.0 m (the ceiling of the 8-12 m first-corner band) simultaneously, and the longest straight has 2.80 m on a 197 m number. None of the three is a violation; all three are one smoothing pass from becoming one. And the pit-lane reverse claim is wrong for the same reason everyone's is - a 20 deg branch is a 160 deg merge driven the other way - though I do not accept the verifier's stated reason for it: its argument that 'a kart exiting T1-reversed tracks out to the RIGHT, straight across the exit-lane junction at 62.0 m' conflates reference frames. Reverse-right is forward-left, and both junctions are on forward-right, so the edge argument actually holds. The angle argument kills it anyway.

Geometry 9/15: closure and heading fine, separation the best in the set, no fake corners. Against it: five of seven corners exceed the measured 1.86 g ceiling on their centreline at the claimed apex (T1 55 m at 119 km/h = 2.026 g, T3 62 at 125 = 1.983, T5 65 at 128 = 1.983, T4 26 at 80 = 1.937, T6 34 at 91 = 1.916), and on the author's own design line the three fast ones land at 99.4%, 99.7% and 100.0% of the ceiling. Three fast corners simultaneously at 100% of one measured number is solving backwards to the limit, and it fails the first time drive.sh re-measures that number. Worse for a validator: the lock sweep's largest row is 58.49 m, and T1, T3 and T5 use design-line radii of 60.3, 66.3 and 69.3 m - all three are extrapolations past the largest radius the data contains.

Elevation 8/20 for the three overlaps and the false both-directions claim above. Credit retained for the derived range (11.42 m from what the ramp can climb), for closing to -3.7e-05 m, for the drainage design actually falling out of the landform (2.0% cross-fall into the hill so a face is never undercut, a -0.70% along-fall to a cut-off drain, the pan draining to its own sump), and for the observation that the same 8% of gradient is two different problems in one lap and the reverse layout swaps which is which - which is the best argument in the set for why elevation earns its place at all.

Run-off 12/15: the >80 deg rule is honoured, including the compound totals at T7 (45+45) and the correct exemptions at T1 45, T2 45, T5 70 and T6 75 - all four of which are given run-off anyway. Widths are sized against named approach speeds (137, 138, 138, 130, 128 km/h) with explicit arrival-at-the-barrier arithmetic: 'a kart that loses it at the 80 km/h apex reaches the barrier at 14 km/h; a kart with no brakes at all reaches it at 113 km/h'. T7's highwall is the best run-off argument anywhere. Docked 3 because T3 needs 82 m of gravel by the document's own figure and gets 35, with the departure-angle defence asserted and never computed; because no verge width appears anywhere; and because La Rampa is the narrowest road on the circuit at 9 m, on made ground carrying 11.42 m of climb, with no embankment specification and no edge protection - and it is the run-up to the reverse layout's second overtaking spot.

Footprint 7/10: 399.4 x 360.4 m = 14.39 ha of box, 93.2 m of lap per hectare - the lowest density in the set, and the author says so ('a low-efficiency plan... a second pass would fold Il Piazzale and La Sponda and take 30 m out of the bounding box'). With T3's 45 m run-off belt the land requirement is about 495 x 456 m = 22.6 ha, the largest of the four by a clear margin. It is defensible: the site is a worked quarry with a stated 300 x 250 m pan and the paddock sits on the old plant yard, so the extra ground is the reason the design exists rather than an overrun. But 22.6 ha is a big property.

Buildability 5/10, the most expensive of the four. 13,564 m2 of ribbon, five distinct widths (9/10/11/12/14) over 9 changes, 11.42 m of relief spread over 14.4 ha, plus three things gentrack.py's ribbon sweep cannot produce and Blender has to bake anyway: a 35 m x 97 m gravel bed at T3 (about 3,400 m2 of 300 mm excavation, and 45 m of run-off belt at that corner alone), a quarry highwall as a modelled asset behind T7, and a 146.3 m made-ground ramp embankment carrying the whole 11.42 m of climb on a 9 m road. Roughly 1.8-2x racecraft's combined bake-area and terrain-mesh cost, and the widest spread of dressed ground of anything here.

Validatability 7/10, the best of the four. Its defects need a speed solver run in both directions - reverse vertical-curve overlaps, braking zone against vertical curve - which is expensive to write, but every one of them is a rule that can be written once and applied to any future track. And terrain is the only proposal that ships something close to a validator specification: a hard_gates block of 15 named booleans (closes_under_1m, longest_straight_under_200, starting_straight_grade_under_2pct, camber_1.5_to_3.0_on_straights, adverse_camber_present, ...). That is the shape ADR-0046's validation list should take.

scores.strongest: The vertical arithmetic is the best-executed in the set and the elevation scale is the only one in four proposals that is a derived quantity rather than a designer's preference. Thirteen gradient changes, all thirteen with R = V^2/K computed at a stated speed, all thirteen arithmetically correct (its verifier reproduces R to 0.5 m and L to 0.05 m on every one), and all thirteen fit inside the segment that carries them with stated before-and-after clearances. The profile closes to 0.00096 m. And the whole profile is scaled by a single factor of 0.80, set by how large a retaining bank the closest pair of track sections can carry - which is the correct causal direction: the elevation is what the plan can support, not what the designer wanted. It is also the most efficient use of ground in the set by a wide margin: 151.7 m of lap per hectare against 93-104 for the other three, on a 232.6 x 368.3 m box, which is what a real 1,300 m Grade 1 circuit actually occupies.
scores.weakest: The plan is too tight for its own elevation and the result is three separate art 7.4 / 7.5 violations that the author identified and then reported the layout as passing anyway. The closest pair is 20.560 m in plan with 10.560 m of clear ground - legal against the 6 m rule - but I measure 8.088 m of height difference across that 10.56 m, a 76.6% face, and it is not a point: roughly 60 m of the start/finish straight faces roughly 60 m of the T7 approach at 45-77%, with three more pairs at 47%, 49% and 46%. Neither side can carry the 1.80 m of even, non-negative-slope verge that art 7.5 requires along the whole length on both sides, let alone the run-off behind it. Then the pit lane: the deceleration lane peels RIGHT at 1150 m and T10 is a LEFT-hander (-52 deg), so the racing line is on the right edge through the entire approach, and the lane sits in it 25.6 m before the braking point. The document's justification - 'the line through T10 is hard left, so a lane peeling right at 1150 m never crosses it' - has a corner entry inverted, and I confirm the verifier's reading independently. The exit lane then rejoins at 195 m onto a 36.72 m link with the field's T2 braking point 22.9 m later, which leaves no room for an 18 deg merge taper and an acceleration lane at once. The author calls that 'the one genuinely uncomfortable thing' and keeps it.
scores.reasoning:
Hard compliance 9/20, the worst in the set, entirely on art 7.4 and 7.5 as above. What passes passes well: length 1300.00, start/finish straight 178.0 m (22 m of margin on the 200 m cap, the most comfortable of the four), 100 m to the first corner and 78 m from the last so both directions clear, first corner 112 deg at 12.0 m, minimum width 10 m - the only layout that never runs at 9 m and therefore the only one with 2 m of width margin over the Grade 1 floor everywhere. Camber 2.0%, banking 2.5-6.0%, no adverse camber. But three regulation breaches, all in articles that describe the parts of a circuit a driver hits rather than drives, is the wrong three to have.

Geometry 8/15: closure 0.001477 m, heading -360.000, zero centreline self-crossings, min separation 20.560 m against a 14 m rule. The horizontal gate passes; see above for why that is the problem rather than the reassurance. Deducted mainly for the racing-line model, which is the proposal's central thesis and is unvalidated: every racing-line radius in the document is exactly Rc + W/2 - 0.7 m, a constant offset with no dependence on the direction change or on the adjacent straights - the hug-the-inside-edge path nobody drives. Recomputing the geometric minimum-curvature line gives T2 94.3 m not 34.3 (2.75x), T10 128.1 not 42.8 (2.99x), T8 283.9 not 114.3 (2.48x), T4 118.5 not 54.3, T6 50.6 not 23.3. The whole point of this lens is that each corner sits on a named rung of the lock sweep - T2 'on #137's boundary at 32.64 m', T6 'the lowest lateral g at the highest steering angle' - and on a defensible line T2 is a 60-90 m corner nowhere near #137 and T6 is a fast corner at low lock, which destroys the T2/T6 pairing. Only T9 (180 deg, hard-bounded), T3 and T1b survive. Also: centreline lateral demand exceeds 1.86 g at four corners (T1b 1.95, T3 2.01, T4 1.99, T10 1.97), which a spline-following probe reads as impossible.

Elevation 13/20 for the arithmetic and the derived scale factor. Docked 7 because 11 of the 13 vertical curves sit on a corner boundary or inside a braking zone - d=539.2 is 0.6 m into T5's turn-in under threshold braking, d=1017.4 is at T9's turn-in at the end of the circuit's biggest braking zone, d=1222.0 is 3.8 m inside T10's exit - and every one is flagged ok:true when the flag reflects only the V^2/K arithmetic and not art 7.2's 'must be adequately increased along approach, release, braking and curved sections'. The overlaps are individually small (largest half-length inside a corner is 4.3 m, every delta under 2.4%), which is why this is a 7-point deduction and not a 12-point one - but nothing in the document says so. And the 0.80 scale factor, derived correctly, was still not enough: it leaves an 8.09 m face between two bits of live track.

Run-off 11/15: the >80 deg rule is honoured on all five qualifying corners (T1 112, T3 150, T5 122, T6 81, T7 83, T9 180) and each is sized against a named approach speed - 135.9 km/h into T1, 133.4 into T9, 112.9 sustained into T3 with the correct observation that a fast corner is left at cornering speed and a shallow angle so it wants a conveyor-fronted barrier rather than depth. T9 gets the largest run-off in the set (22 m of asphalt plus 3 m of gravel) and it is the corner that needs it. The disclosure is the best of the four: grass measures 0.286 g against 1.156 g on asphalt at M3b, which implies stopping distances far longer than any width quoted, 'which means the real answer is that these run-offs work by reducing impact speed and not by stopping the kart' - and that distinction appears in none of the numbers, said out loud. Docked for T6 sitting at 81 deg, one degree over the threshold that makes axis run-off mandatory, on an angle the author admits came out of the heading-closure solve rather than a decision; for T7 being explicitly under-built for the reverse layout (sized against 102.9 km/h, approached at 133.6 reversed) and left that way; and for no verge number anywhere.

Footprint 6/10, and it is the most interesting trade in the whole set. 232.6 x 368.3 m = 8.57 ha is by far the most efficient plan here - 151.7 m of lap per hectare against 93-104 for the others - and with a 30 m belt the land requirement is about 293 x 428 m = 12.5 ha, which is exactly the size of a real European Grade 1 circuit of this length. On paper it is the only one of four that a landowner would recognise. On site it is not buildable as drawn, because the density is bought with a 60 m long, 8 m high, 76% face between two live sections. Half marks: the ambition is right, the execution needs about 12 m more plan separation at one pair, and that is a full re-solve.

Buildability 6/10: 26 segments and 12 corners (most in the set), 13,620 m2 of ribbon, 11 width changes across 10-14 m with no taper length given for any of them - the 11->14->10 across T9 is a 4 m step out and back over 44 m of arc, and the 14 m entry is the entire overtaking argument. Smallest terrain extent of the four (8.57 ha at 8.47 m of relief) which is genuinely cheap. The killer is the retaining structure: roughly 60 m of 8 m high wall at 76%, with live track on both sides of it, is a bespoke asset the ribbon sweeper cannot make, and a lightmap bake across a near-vertical face with asphalt above and below it is exactly where shadow acne and lumel starvation show up.

Validatability 4/10, the hardest of the four to write a check for. The binding failure is invisible to every gate this project has or that the brief specified: the 14 m centreline rule is purely horizontal and passes 20.560 m without comment, and finding the real defect needs a 3D separation test plus a slope-between-sections test that nothing in the codebase does. The author says this himself - 'the brief's separation rule is purely horizontal and would have passed this silently'. By ADR-0046's own standard, a track that loads and cannot be raced is worse than one that refuses to load, and this is the layout that would load.

best_corners.corner: T7 (the uphill hairpin into the old highwall)
best_corners.why: The only mandatory axial run-off in four proposals that is free from the site. 45+45 deg compound correctly totalled to a 90 deg direction change, so art 7.5's run-off is mandatory, and the axis points straight up the hill into an existing quarry face: 6 m of apron at the art 7.5 10% up-slope cap, 22 m of rising gravel, tire barrier against rock. It costs nothing to build and nothing to model, and the up-slope does the decelerating that 0.286 g grass cannot.
best_corners.graft: Put the winner's tightest hairpin at the top of its climb with the axis of the direction change aimed at a cut face, and let the run-off rise into it. Carry terrain's arithmetic style with it - 'a kart with no brakes reaches the barrier at X km/h' - rather than a width.

best_corners.corner: the vertical-curve margin policy (VC1 1.42x, VC2 1.91x, VC3 1.34x over minimum)
best_corners.why: Not a corner, the most important thing in the set. Art 7.2 says R 'must be adequately increased' near approach, release, braking and curved sections and gives no number. Terrain answered 'exactly the minimum, there was no reason not to' and produced three overlap failures. Instrument sat 11 of 13 curves on corner boundaries at the minimum. Rhythm picked a multiplier per curve, applied it, and published what it cost - about 3 m of available elevation range.
best_corners.graft: Adopt the multiplier as a rule in ARCHITECTURE section 11: 1.3x minimum outside named sections, 1.9x or better inside them, and state the elevation range it costs. Then a validator has a number to check instead of an adverb.

best_corners.why: 111.75 m of -4.38% descent to 143.7 km/h - the only place in either direction the kart reaches top speed - into a 48.5 m braking zone, a 10 m entry, and an exit onto 319 m of climbing full throttle. It is the best overtaking corner on the property and it does not exist forwards, which is exactly what GAMEDESIGN section 10 asks a reverse layout to be: content, not a mirror.
best_corners.graft: Site one hairpin at the bottom of the longest descent so that reversing the direction moves the tow rather than reflecting it. Pair it with racecraft's honest disclosure that the same corner's brake-failure case needs 91.7 m of gravel forward and 101.5 m reversed, and that neither is built.

best_corners.why: At the legal minimum vertical radius, a_vert = v^2/R = v^2/(V^2/K) = K/12.96 m/s2 regardless of speed. So a legal Grade 1 kart circuit can never swing tire load by more than -11.8% over any crest or +15.7% in any compression, at any speed, and the article's 'increase R near braking and curves' only reduces it. This settles ARCHITECTURE section 11's claim that elevation 'loads the tires' - it does, by at most a sixth of static, and only in the slow parts.
best_corners.graft: Put it in ARCHITECTURE section 11 as the reason elevation is a visibility and braking-distance lever on a kart circuit and not a grip lever. It kills a whole class of future design argument before anybody spends a session on it.

best_corners.why: 14 m radius through 180 deg with the road going 11 -> 14 -> 10 m across the corner, a 39.4 m braking zone from 133.4 km/h, and 22 m of axial asphalt run-off plus 3 m of gravel - the largest run-off in the set on the corner that most needs it. It is the only corner in four proposals where the width IS the overtaking argument rather than a note beside it, and the brief is explicit that a kart overtaking spot is made of entry width, not braking length.
best_corners.graft: Take the 11 -> 14 -> 10 profile and the 22 m axial run-off. Fix what instrument omits: a taper length for each width step. A 4 m step out and back over 44 m of arc with no stated transition is not a specification, and 'all changes in banking are to be made over an appropriate distance' has an obvious analogue for width.

best_corners.why: 50 m radius through 150 deg, 4.17 s of sustained load, and it changes hand with the layout - forward it loads the 2.43 g rollover side, reversed the 2.81 g side, at the same 1.84 g. That is a 15.6% margin change on the same asphalt at the same speed, which is the cleanest A/B the two layouts can offer for the section 6 inside-rear-lift model, and it costs nothing to author.
best_corners.graft: Whichever layout wins needs one long constant-radius corner around 50-55 m held for over 4 s, so the forward and reverse layouts differ by a measurable rollover margin rather than by vibes. Cross-check against the sweep's largest measured row (58.49 m) so the radius is inside the data rather than extrapolated past it.

best_corners.why: The same axis is sized twice - 8 m asphalt plus 14 m grass against a 106 km/h forward approach, 12 m plus 26 m against a 132 km/h reversed one - with the v^2 energy ratio stated (1.55x). It is the concrete demonstration that a reverse layout is geometry and furniture and not a spline direction, which is what ADR-0046 asserts and what three of four documents assert back without an example.
best_corners.graft: Make every corner's runoff field a pair, one entry per layout, sized by v^2 against that layout's own approach speed, with the larger one built. That also catches instrument's T7 defect automatically - sized for 102.9 km/h forward, approached at 133.6 reversed, and left that way.

best_corners.why: The range is not a taste call: La Rampa plus the entry half of T7 is 146.3 m of climbing road, 146.3 m is what the 200 m straight cap allows there, and 7.81% is the steepest sustained gradient the design accepts - so 11.42 m is what the circuit can climb back and no more. Two regulations meeting produce the number. Instrument's 0.80 scale factor is the same idea derived from a different constraint; racecraft's 14.587 m and rhythm's 7.393 m are chosen.
best_corners.graft: Derive the range from the return climb rather than picking it, and publish the constraint that set it. It is a one-line justification that turns the single most arbitrary number in a track file into a measurement.

concerns: The brief's self-intersection rule is purely horizontal and it passed the single worst regulation failure in the set silently. Instrument's closest pair is 20.560 m in plan - comfortably over the 14 m rule - with 10.560 m of clear ground and 8.088 m of height difference, a 76.6% face, over roughly 60 m of both sections. Art 7.5 requires 1.80 m of even verge with no negative slope on both sides for the whole length and caps run-off up-slope at 10%; neither side of that face can carry either. The rule needs a 3D form: clear ground between asphalt edges AND the slope between the two surfaces no steeper than 10%, unless a retaining structure is explicitly specified as track furniture. As written, a designer is rewarded for stacking the circuit vertically.

The 40 m arc-separation exemption is where three of four layouts' minima land: racecraft 40.02 m, terrain 40.03 m, rhythm 40.07 m. That is not gaming - a corner's own turn-in and exit tangents are naturally about 40 m apart on a kart-scale radius - but it means the gate is being passed at the edge of its own exclusion window and is measuring almost nothing at those three layouts. Raise the exemption to 60 m, or exclude pairs that belong to the same corner explicitly.

The brief specifies no racing-line convention and every layout invented one: instrument used Rc + W/2 - 0.7 m (hug the inside edge), terrain used Rc + (W - 1.4)/2, racecraft capped line radius at 2x the centreline radius, rhythm used a chord-and-offset formula. On identical geometry these differ by up to 3x - terrain's own risks note says T2's idealised line is 143 m against its 26.8 m model. Since every '#137 boundary', every apex speed and every '1.86 g ceiling' claim is downstream of that convention, four proposals were scored on four different physics. The convention belongs in the brief, and the closed form racecraft's verifier used (R_line = R + (w/2)(1+cos(t/2))/(1-cos(t/2))) is a reasonable candidate for the free case.

'Longest straight max 200 m' is checked geometrically and defeated in effect by all four. Continuous full-throttle runs, merging straights across any corner of centreline radius >= 80 m: terrain 196.9 m, instrument 219.9 m, racecraft 237.8 m (380 m by its verifier's own speed profile, because T6 is also flat), rhythm 354.5 m. The rule exists to cap terminal speed. Ask instead for the longest run with no braking event, computed from the speed profile, and cap that - otherwise a designer buys 150 m of legality with an R=90 m kink that does not corner.

The lock sweep the entire corner vocabulary rests on varies THROTTLE as well as lock across its three 0.25-lock rows (0.30, 0.60, 1.00). So 'settled radius 18.99 / 32.64 / 58.49 m' confounds radius, speed, normal load and throttle, and cannot separate them. Every one of the four layouts built its corner ladder on interpolations across those three points, and rhythm's risks name it as the biggest error source in its corner table. That deserves a probe with one variable moving before any of it becomes track.json.

The sweep's largest measured radius is 58.49 m, and three layouts place corners at 60-70 m of line radius (terrain T1 60.3, T3 66.3, T5 69.3) - all extrapolations past the data. The brief's own reference table then quotes r=80 m at 137.5 km/h and r=120 m as flat, which are v^2/r figures at 1.86 g and not measurements. Separately, the brief's headline 1.86 g and the sweep's own best row 1.84 g disagree; racecraft's risks point out that this moves T3's apex by 0.7 km/h. Say which number is binding.

Nothing in the brief asks for a verge width and all four omitted it. Art 7.5's 1.80 m of compact verge with no negative slope, grass or compacted over at least 1 m of it, is the one requirement that applies to the whole lap rather than to corners, and it is the requirement instrument's terrace actually breaks. It should be a per-segment field with a floor, not corner prose.

The pit lane does not reverse in any of the four, and the brief never says it has to. A deceleration lane branching at 20-25 deg to the direction of travel is a 155-160 deg merge driven the other way, over art 7.2's 30 deg cap, regardless of which edge it is on. Only racecraft worked it out and said so; terrain claims its junctions are fine in reverse and rhythm and instrument do not check. If GAMEDESIGN section 10 makes the reverse layout first-class, the brief should state that the pit complex is geometry per layout, not shared furniture - which is a real cost worth knowing before a layout is picked.

Elevation closure is gated at 0.05 m but only over the segment grade list. Racecraft publishes a second profile - the vertical-curve schedule at its published stations and transition lengths - which does not close (+0.601 m) and disagrees with the first by up to 2.095 m, and reported the one that passes. gentrack.py will consume exactly one z(s). The gate should be on the profile the sweeper would actually eat, and ADR-0046 should say which of the two fields is authoritative.

I do not accept one finding in terrain.verify.json. Its reverse pit-lane violation argues that 'a kart exiting T1-reversed tracks out to the RIGHT, straight across the exit-lane junction at 62.0 m'. Reverse-right is forward-left, and both terrain junctions are on the forward-right edge, so the edge argument actually holds in reverse. The junctions do fail in reverse - on the merge angle, as above - but the reason given is a reference-frame error, and the same error would wrongly clear or wrongly condemn junctions on any future layout. Worth correcting before it is copied into a validator.
summary: Four layouts, four 'major issues' verdicts, and the ranking is inside two points across the top three. Every one of them closes (0.0005 to 0.017 m against a 1 m gate), every one holds -360 or +360 deg of heading exactly, every one lands in the 1,100-1,400 m band, and every one keeps a legal minimum width, a legal camber and a legal banking. What separates them is what happens once you stop checking plan geometry. Rhythm wins on cost-to-legal: its vertical work is the only one that reads 'adequately increased' as a multiplier and pays for it, its forward geometry is the cleanest to check, and its defects are field edits - raise two vertical radii, relabel T4's cliff relation from 'on the boundary' to 5.1 km/h past it, delete an invented 18.4 m clearance that measures 152.6 m, reconcile a 0.586 s sector sum. None of them moves a control point. Its worst fault is conceptual and it is the reverse layout: a crest is a crest driven either way, K does not swap, and 'checked, all six pass' is not true. Racecraft is second on the strength of the best run-off work here - required gravel against built gravel, per corner, with the assumptions named - the only forward pit lane whose geometry I could verify without argument, the only recognition anywhere that a pit lane does not reverse, and a general derivation (load swing capped at -11.8%/+15.7% at any speed) that belongs in ARCHITECTURE. It loses on publishing two elevation profiles that describe different roads, one of which misses closure by 0.601 m, which for a pipeline that sweeps a ribbon along one z(s) is a source-of-truth failure and not a rounding note. Terrain has the best hard-gate record and the only longest straight that is also its longest full-throttle run, and it is the layout sold on elevation whose elevation is the worst-executed - a claimed +1.5 m margin at La Conca that is -3.48 m because its braking arithmetic is out by 2.3x, a claimed 31 m lead-in between two crests that is 1.729 m, a 13.21 m vertical-curve overlap in reverse, and a flat 'both directions now pass' that is false. It is also the most expensive thing here to build: about 22.6 ha of land, 11.42 m of relief across it, a 3,400 m2 gravel bed, a modelled highwall and a 146 m made-ground embankment - call it 1.8-2x racecraft, which is the cheapest at 17 segments and 12,244 m2 of ribbon. Instrument is last and it is the most instructive failure. Its vertical arithmetic is the best in the set (13 of 13 correct, 13 of 13 fitting their segment, profile closing to 0.96 mm, the whole thing scaled by a factor derived from what the plan can hold) and its plan is the most efficient piece of land anyone drew, 151.7 m of lap per hectare against 93-104. It is last because that density is bought with a 60 m long, 8 m high, 76% face between the start/finish straight and the T7 approach, where art 7.5 needs 1.80 m of non-negative-slope verge on both sides; because its deceleration lane peels right into the racing line of a left-hander on a justification that has the corner inverted; because its exit lane merges 22.9 m before the field's braking point; and because the racing-line model its entire lock-sweep thesis rests on is the hug-the-inside-edge path, off by 1.9x to 3.0x on seven of twelve corners. It is also the hardest to validate: the brief's own separation rule passed the 20.560 m pair without comment, and catching the real defect needs a 3D separation-and-slope test that nothing in this project has. To ADR-0046's standard - a track that loads and cannot be raced is worse than one that refuses to load - instrument is the one that would load.
